title: Ἀθηναῖος χρεωφειλέτης
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 10 (= Perry 5). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀθήνησι χρεωφειλέτης ἀνὴρ ἀπαιτούμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ δανειστοῦ τὸ χρέος τὸ μὲν πρῶτον παρεκάλει ἀναβολὴν αὐτῷ δοῦναι, ἀπορεῖν φάσκων.
sentences.tr: Athēnēsi chreōpheiletēs anēr apaitoumenos hypo tou daneistou to chreos to men prōton parekalei anabolēn autōi dounai, aporein phaskōn.
sentences.l: At Athens a man in debt, being dunned for the debt by his creditor, at first was begging him to grant him a postponement, asserting that he was without means.
sentences.i: At Athens a man in debt, pressed by his creditor for the money, at first begged for an extension, claiming he had nothing.
sentences.n: Ἀθήνησι is a locative, “at Athens” — an old case surviving in a handful of place-names. ἀπαιτούμενος is passive yet keeps τὸ χρέος in the accusative: a verb with two objects can hold the second one when it goes passive. τὸ μὲν πρῶτον, “at first,” is already promising the ὡς δέ of the next sentence.

sentences.t: Ὡς δὲ οὐκ ἔπειθε, προσαγαγὼν ὗν ἣν εἶχε μόνην, παρόντος αὐτοῦ, ἐπώλει.
sentences.tr: Hōs de ouk epeithe, prosagagōn hyn hēn eiche monēn, parontos autou, epōlei.
sentences.l: But when he was not persuading him, having brought forward the sow which he had as his only one, with him standing by, he set about selling her.
sentences.i: When that did not persuade him, he brought out the one sow he owned and offered her for sale with the creditor standing there.
sentences.n: παρόντος αὐτοῦ is a genitive absolute: a noun and participle set in the genitive and standing outside the sentence's grammar to give the attendant circumstances, “he being present.” It is one of the commonest constructions in this prose. ἔπειθε and ἐπώλει are imperfects of attempt — “was trying to persuade,” “was putting up for sale.”

sentences.t: Ὠνητοῦ δὲ προσελθόντος καὶ διερωτῶντος εἰ τοκὰς ἡ ὗς εἴη, ἐκεῖνος ἔφη μὴ μόνον αὐτὴν τίκτειν, ἀλλὰ καὶ παραδόξως· τοῖς μὲν γὰρ μυστηρίοις θήλεα ἀποκύειν, τοῖς δὲ Παναθηναίοις ἄρσενα.
sentences.tr: Ōnētou de proselthontos kai dierōtōntos ei tokas hē hys eiē, ekeinos ephē mē monon autēn tiktein, alla kai paradoxōs: tois men gar mystēriois thēlea apokyein, tois de Panathēnaiois arsena.
sentences.l: And a buyer having come up and asking closely whether the sow was a breeder, that man said that she not only bore young, but even wonderfully: for at the Mysteries she brought forth females, and at the Panathenaia males.
sentences.i: A buyer came up and pressed him whether the sow bred; the man said she not only bred but bred wonderfully — at the Mysteries she bore females, at the Panathenaia males.
sentences.n: Two participles in one genitive absolute (Ὠνητοῦ … προσελθόντος καὶ διερωτῶντος). εἴη is the optative Greek uses for an indirect question set in past-time narrative, in place of the direct ἐστί. μή, not οὐ, is the negative with an infinitive. The lie is a calendar joke: the Eleusinian Mysteries were the autumn festival of Demeter and Persephone, at which each initiate sacrificed a piglet, and the Panathenaia was Athena's summer festival — so the sow is claimed to time the sex of her litters to the feast.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ ἐκπλαγέντος πρὸς τὸν λόγον, ὁ δανειστὴς εἶπεν· « Ἀλλὰ μὴ θαύμαζε· αὕτη γάρ σοι καὶ Διονυσίοις ἐρίφους τέξεται. »
sentences.tr: Tou de ekplagentos pros ton logon, ho daneistēs eipen: « Alla mē thaumaze: hautē gar soi kai Dionysiois eriphous texetai. »
sentences.l: And he being astounded at the account, the creditor said: « But do not marvel: for she will bear you kids at the Dionysia as well. »
sentences.i: When the buyer was struck dumb at this, the creditor said, « Do not be astonished: she will bear you goat-kids at the Dionysia into the bargain. »
sentences.n: A third genitive absolute, and the point of the fable: the creditor caps the lie instead of exposing it, since a sale is his only way to be paid. Goats were Dionysus' animal and his sacrifice; an ancient tradition, itself a guess, further connects the goat with his dramatic contests by way of τραγῳδία, “goat-song.” Either way the sow is made to oblige with kids in season. μή, not οὐ, is the negative of a prohibition.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι πολλοὶ διὰ τὸ ἴδιον κέρδος οὐκ ὀκνοῦσιν οὐδὲ τοῖς ἀδυνατοις ψευδομαρτυρεῖν.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti polloi dia to idion kerdos ouk oknousin oude tois adynatois pseudomartyrein.
sentences.l: The story shows that many, because of their own gain, do not shrink even from bearing false witness to impossible things.
sentences.i: The story shows that many, for their own profit, will not scruple to bear false witness even to what cannot be.
sentences.n: διά with the accusative gives the reason, “because of”; with the genitive it would mean “through.” ψευδομαρτυρεῖν is the courtroom word for giving false testimony — an Athenian's word, apt for an Athenian story. τοῖς ἀδυνάτοις is taken here as neuter, “to things impossible”; the masculine, “the powerless,” is grammatically open but does not fit what the fable has just shown.
